desc: Created using Procreate Dreams. This is a frame by frame animation exploring nature and man's new relationship with it.

Three illustrations commissioned by Positive News to accompany a feature on offline dating: the different ways people are meeting, connecting, and building relationships outside the apps. The brief asked for images that could hold the full tonal range of the subject: the awkwardness, the hope, the occasional absurdity. Published across print and digital.

Illustrations for The Telegraph accompanying an article on ending friendships: the specific difficulty of breaking up with people you've outgrown rather than wronged. The work ran as animated GIFs online and as static images in print, which meant the characters had to carry emotional weight in both a still frame and in motion. Dry, a little melancholy, and precise enough to feel true rather than illustrative.

A collection of illustrations created for the relaunched Kueski Pay app and website, one of Latin America's largest financial service providers. The aim was to bring warmth and approachability to fintech, which is an area that usually features less approachable advertising. The work comprised hero imagery and modular drop-in characters, built to show Kueski as a presence in everyday life, not just a payment mechanism. It's playful, colourful, and designed to scale across app interfaces, digital billboards, and social channels.

Out-of-home illustration and animation for Humantold, a mental health platform built for New Yorkers. The work rolled out across the iconic New York subway, which was a very deliberate choice for a campaign about accessing therapy in the city that never sleeps. The characters were drawn from the specific area of 'city stress' like construction noise, ghosting, the relentless pace of work and play. They were designed to catch people in that brief stillness of a platform wait, and make the idea of talking to someone feel genuinely reachable.

A printed onboarding booklet for AO, the UK's largest online white goods retailer, aimed at new delivery drivers joining the fleet. The illustrations walked through the process of a delivery shift: the steps, the expectations, the moments of contact with customers. The challenge was making a functional document feel human rather than bureaucratic: characters and scenarios that reflect what the job actually looks and feels like, rather than an instruction manual with pictures.

An animated campaign for APO Discounter, one of Germany's largest online pharmacies, promoting their app to existing users. The brief called for something warm and everyday: illustrations of the kind of people who actually use the app, in the kind of moments where it makes their life easier. Alex designed the characters; KITCHEN brought them to life as the brand commercial. Light, slightly surreal, and deliberately far from the clinical aesthetic that pharmacy advertising tends to default to.

A series of characters and illustrations for Cadooz, an employee rewards and benefits platform, created for their website redesign. The brief was to convey the breadth of what Cadooz offers (rewards that work for every kind of person at every size of company) without defaulting to generic workplace imagery. The solution was a cast of characters: abstract figures alongside human ones, each drawn with enough specificity to feel like actual people rather than demographic stand-ins.

A series of illustrated cards created for Apple's Today Tab, the editorial front page of the App Store and Podcast Store. Each card was built around a specific app or curated set, using character work and bold composition to hold attention in a space where illustration more often competes with photography and UI. The cards themselves were featured across multiple regions, which meant the work had to read cleanly at small scale while also holding up as a full-bleed feature.

Illustration and animation for General Mills Mott's Fruit Snacks, supporting a campaign encouraging reading in communities with fewer resources. Each box came with a free book, and my characters running across both the packaging and the books themselves. I wanted the figures to feel like proper story characters rather than brand mascots. The campaign made the snack box itself part of the reading experience, with illustration appealing to children before the book was even opened.

An interactive installation for the Adidas Yoga X Oceans campaign, which went live in their flagship Oxford Street store. A camera tracked visitors attempting a yoga pose; once the pose was held, it captured the moment and sent them an illustrated version of themselves (drawn in my signature character style) directly to their email. The project was a fun combination of retail activation, illustration, and real-time personalisation, with the characters generated from live photography rather than any pre-drawn template.

A winter travel campaign for CLEAR Plus, the biometric airport security service, spanning motion, gifting, and in-airport installations. The brief was to bottle the particular emotional register of holiday travel: the stress of the queue, the relief of getting through it, and the warmth of what's waiting at the other end. Character work and animation by Alex, directed by KITCHEN. The campaign leaned into the togetherness angle: the idea that what makes holiday travel worthwhile isn't the journey but who you're making it for.

A campaign for First Bus explaining the tap-on tap-off contactless payment system to passengers across the UK. The illustrations appeared on buses and across the web, and were designed to make a behaviour change feel natural and non-preachy rather than instructional. Characters in transit, mid-journey, going through the motion organically. The work had to read clearly at poster scale and compress into a digital format without losing the warmth of the original drawings.

To help people power through 2020, I was approached by Spotify to build a High Intensity Interval Training programme timed to 30-second clips, which were all the right tempo for each exercise. Guided by my characters and animated by KITCHEN, users moved through the workout to the soundtrack of voices from Spotify's podcast talent. The character had to do a lot - be motivating without being annoying, come across as slightly absurd, but also convincing and compelling enough to follow for a full workout session.

A clean, simple set of looping animations produced for ThinkArtfully, a highly esteemed creative production agency. The work was used across their own brand materials and digital presence. These motion pieces needed to represent the agency's range and energy without settling on a single visual register. With frame-by-frame character animation, each loop is designed to feel considered and complete rather than simply decorative.

A set of illustrations for Positive News on the theme of urban nature: the ways people are bringing green space, growing, and wildness into cities. Scenes of everyday life inflected by plants, allotments, window boxes, and the small acts of rewilding that happen in dense environments. Commissioned for print.

Editorial illustrations for Philadelphia Magazine on sustainable living: the practical, everyday approaches to reducing environmental impact. Characters drawn from domestic and urban life, placed in scenes that make eco choices feel normal and achievable rather than aspirational or preachy. Published in print.

A vinyl window installation for Art of Ping Pong, a creative event space and hospitality venue. The illustration wrapped the street-facing windows: large-format character work designed to signal the playfulness of what was happening inside and draw people in off the street. Bold line work and a flat colour palette that read clearly at scale and held up under the variable light conditions of a busy London exterior.

A large-scale experiential installation for Hyundai Mall in South Korea, reimagining Alice in Wonderland in a contemporary illustrated environment. The work moved from character drawings into physical space, which featured giant wall wraps, inflatable structures, and in-building graphics. This meant my illustration had to hold its own at a scale where every line and colour decision read several metres wide. The visual approach drew on bold vector line work and a strong palette designed for both immersive environments and digital backdrops across the event space.

A limited-edition T-shirt design for Levi's, commissioned to mark the Royal Wedding. The brief sat at an unusual intersection, British cultural iconography filtered through streetwear, and needed to feel like a genuine collector piece rather than a souvenir. Vector illustration optimised for screen printing on premium denim and textiles, with a graphic sensibility that could sit comfortably in Levi's archive of artist collaborations.
